blocks.text: Master Lianchi: Canceled in One Stroke

inline.s: On New Year's Eve of the yichou year of the Jiajing reign (1565), Master Lianchi asked his wife, Lady Tang, to brew tea. As Lady Tang carried the tea to the desk, it slipped from her hands and fell to the floor. Seeing the beloved heirloom jade cup shattered, the Master smiled and said:
“All causes and conditions must eventually disperse.”

The next year, he bade Lady Tang farewell, saying: “Affection cannot last forever, and in birth and death no one can take another's place. I am going to leave home; make good arrangements for yourself.” Lady Tang, likewise free and easy, said: “You go first; once I have arranged the household, I too shall leave home.” Thereupon the Master composed the verses “Canceled in One Stroke” and left home.

[Canceled in one stroke] This is an old phrase from settling accounts, meaning to wipe out a debt that has been repaid with one stroke of the brush; later it was extended to mean canceling everything entirely — wiped out in one stroke. For example, the late-Tang Daoist Lü Dongbin, in his awakening lyric “Qinyuan Chun,” wrote: “Enough, enough — turn back early, and wipe away the romantic past with one stroke.”

“Parental kindness is heavy as hills and peaks; offerings of five cauldrons and three beasts cannot repay its due. When one's parents leave the dust and grime, the child's duty is then complete. Cha! The great cause of leaving home — how can worldly feeling fathom it through? Filial sons and worthy grandsons should investigate true emptiness; therefore the five-colored golden insignia are canceled in one stroke.”

Parents' kindness is weighty as hills and peaks; the five cauldrons and three beasts are not enough to repay it. One must surely rescue both parents from birth and death before the child's filial duty is complete. Cha! The great cause of leaving home — how could the understanding of ordinary beings see through it? Truly filial sons and worthy grandsons should investigate the true reality of all dharmas (only by attaining the Way oneself can one rescue one's parents from the sea of birth and death); therefore the five-colored golden insignia of honor to one's parents and glory to one's ancestors are canceled in one stroke.

[Five cauldrons and three beasts] A description of extremely lavish offerings. [Five cauldrons] In ancient sacrificial rites, a grandee used five cauldrons. [Three beasts] Ox, sheep, and pig. [When one's parents leave the dust and grime, the child's duty is then complete] This means: when one's parents have ended birth and death (left the dust and grime), only then have the children truly fulfilled their filial duty. [Cha
chā

] An exclamation; here it is a blow to the head (a sudden shout of awakening). [True emptiness] The true reality of all dharmas. [The true reality of all dharmas] The actual state of all things. The Buddha Repository Sutra says:
“What is called the true reality of all dharmas? It is that all dharmas are ultimately empty and without anything there is.”
(For details, see
The True Reality of All Dharmas
[Five-colored golden insignia] The official robes of high officials in ancient times; here it refers to attaining success and fame, honoring one's parents, and bringing glory to one's ancestors.
Master Hanshan said:

“What parents throughout the world hope for in their children is that they attain fame and honor their parents; thus they regard the support of the three beasts and five cauldrons as fulfilling filial piety. Little do they know that the richer the support, the deeper the suffering; this burdens one's parents and is not true filial piety. Thus our Buddha, the World-Honored One, regarded the golden wheel
(scorned the position of the wheel-turning king)

as worthless, left his parents, abandoned the royal palace, practiced austerities in the snowy mountains, and in six years attained the Way, becoming honored in the three realms and revered by humans and gods. Had he not cast aside the most precious things and cut off great love, how could he have won the imperishable work of long kalpas? Hence it is said: ‘The greatly filial Śākya, the World-Honored One, repaid his parents' kindness across kalpas.’ Is this not taking the realization of the unborn and the universal deliverance of living beings as the ground of repaying them? The Buddha taught the great precepts, beginning with: filial piety is called the precept. That is, to be filial to one's parents, filial to one's teachers and the monastic order and the Three Jewels, filial to the supreme Way, and filial to all living beings. Therefore, one who truly studies and practices the Buddha's path will regard all living beings as one's parents of many lives — how could one not repay the parents of this one life
(how could one fail to repay the kindness of this life's parents)
(The Dream Journey Collection
, “Instructing Layman Wang Zi'an on Sending His Son to Leave Home”)

blocks.text: 2. The Chapter on Husband and Wife

inline.s: “Phoenix mates and paired lovebirds, when will the tangle of affection ever end? Living ghosts keep each other company in disguise, and when the affinity ends they still part. Cha! For your two hearts entwined, you wear the cangue and carry the shackles. See through the enemy — each seeks a gate of escape; therefore the fish-and-water couple is canceled in one stroke.”

Phoenix mates and paired lovebirds — when will the tangle of affection ever end? Are you not just a pair of living ghosts keeping each other company in disguise, parting when the affinity ends? Cha! For your two hearts' tender entanglement, you wear the cangue and drag the shackles. See through the enemy who comes to collect the debt — each seeks a gate of liberation and walks away; therefore the fish-and-water couple is canceled in one stroke.
[Phoenix mates and paired lovebirds] Refers to the intimacy of man and woman, harmonious companions like phoenix and lovebird. [Shackles
chǒu
] A kind of ancient manacle. [Entwined
chóu móu

] Deep, tender, lingering affection: two hearts entwined. [Enemy] A foe who has come for revenge. “Husband and wife are enemies” means that each drags the other down, suffering endlessly in the cycle of birth and death. The Śūraṅgama Sūtra says:
“You love my mind, I cherish your form; by this cause and condition, through a hundred thousand kalpas, we remain ever entangled.”

The way to resolve it is to enter the gate of liberation, turning lovers into companions on the Way. [Each seeks a gate of escape] Each seeks the gate for ending birth and death (the Buddha's gate) and walks through it.

blocks.text: 3. The Chapter on Children and Grandchildren

inline.s: “The body is like a sore and a wen
(yóu)

; do not make distant worries for your children and grandchildren. Recall the Dou of Mount Yan — does he still remain today? Cha! After all there comes an end; all returns to nothing after. Who recognizes the person himself, unchanging as of old for myriad ages? Therefore the fine sons and grandsons are canceled in one stroke.”

The physical body is filthy and painful like a sore or a wen; do not make distant worries for your children and grandchildren. Recall the Dou of Mount Yan, who taught his five sons and made their names known throughout the land — do they still remain today? Cha! After all there comes an end; all returns to nothing after; on the road to the yellow springs one walks alone. Who recognizes the person himself (the self-nature), unchanging as of old for myriad ages (never aging and never dying)? Therefore the fine sons and grandsons are canceled in one stroke.

[The Dou of Mount Yan] This is Dou Yujun, of the Later Jin period of the Five Dynasties. His native home was Yuyang in Jizhou, in the region of Mount Yan, so later generations respectfully called him Dou Yanshan — the old custom of using a place name in place of a personal name as a mark of respect. He was strict in family discipline and had five sons, all of whom excelled in both learning and conduct; people of the time praised them as the “Five Dragons of the Dou family.” All passed the jinshi examination and became pillars of the state. The Three Character Classic says: “Dou Yanshan, with right methods, taught his five sons, all of whom made their names known.” [Do they still remain today] “Where are the generals and ministers of old and new? A mound of wild grass covers all that's left.” (The Song of the Good End, from The Dream of the Red Chamber) [All returns to nothing after] When the last breath fails to come, one walks the yellow springs alone; ultimately speaking, what descendants or heirs are there at all?

[Who recognizes the person himself] Who realizes that the self-nature alone is truly oneself? Living beings are deluded, falsely taking the physical body for the self, and do not realize that the self-nature is who they really are; hence there is the cycle of birth and death. The Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment says:

“All living beings, from time without beginning, are variously inverted, like a person who has lost his way and mistakes the four directions, falsely taking the four great elements for the appearance of the self and the shadows of the six sense-objects for the appearance of their own mind. It is like diseased eyes that see flowers in the sky and a second moon. ...... From this false existence they revolve in birth and death; hence it is called ignorance.”

Translation: All living beings, from time without beginning, are deluded in the self-nature and give rise to all kinds of inversion, taking the false for the true. This is like a person who has lost his bearings, taking north for south and east for west: he falsely takes the physical body formed of the four great elements of earth, water, fire, and wind as the appearance of the self, and the discriminating mind by which the six sense-roots engage the six sense-objects (the shadows of the six sense-objects) as the appearance of his own mind. It is like eyes that are blurred, falsely seeing flowers in the sky and a second moon.

Because of their inverted delusion, living beings falsely take the illusory body and mind as truly existing and cling to them as the self; thus they revolve endlessly in birth and death. Hence it is called ignorance.

[The four great elements] The great element of earth, the great element of water, the great element of fire, and the great element of wind. Earth has solidity as its nature, water has moisture as its nature, fire has warmth as its nature, and wind has movement as its nature. All material things in the world possess the four natures of solidity, moisture, warmth, and movement, and so are called “great elements.” The physical body is composed of the four great elements; here “the four great elements” refers to the physical body. [The shadows of the six sense-objects] The various thoughts produced when the six sense-roots engage the six sense-objects; since these thoughts are all illusory and unreal, they are called the shadows of the six sense-objects — the illusory shadows of the six sense-objects. [Fine sons and grandsons] A term of praise for a person's descendants. When children and grandchildren are simultaneously distinguished and flourishing, it is called “orchid and cassia blooming together.”

blocks.text: 4. The Chapter on Fame and Achievement

inline.s: “Standing alone atop the turtle's head, say not this is a man's season of triumph. The golden seal hangs like a dipper, its show of power cannot last long. Cha! How much striving in vain, from a boy's face to hoary head. When the dream of yellow millet ends, one smiles at the nothingness; therefore wealth, rank, and renown are canceled in one stroke.”

Standing alone atop the turtle's head — say not this is a man's season of triumph. The golden seal hangs like a dipper, but its show of power cannot last long. Cha! How much striving in vain, as a boy's face turns in a blink to a hoary head. When the dream of yellow millet wakes, look and see what remains; therefore wealth, rank, and renown are canceled in one stroke.

[Standing alone atop the turtle's head] “The turtle's head” is the relief carving of a giant turtle on the steps before the palace gate. When the list of successful jinshi candidates was posted, the top candidate (zhuangyuan) stood upon it to receive the announcement. [Golden seal] A golden official seal, held in ancient times by the chancellor, the grand councilor, the grand commandant, the grand minister of works, the grand tutor, the grand preceptor, the grand protector, the generals of the front, rear, left, and right, and the empresses and consorts of the six palaces. Later it referred to high office and rank. [The golden seal hangs like a dipper] A dipper-sized golden seal hung on one's person by a purple ribbon, describing a display of great power. [Its show of power cannot last long] Wealth, rank, and glory, literary brilliance, and perfect happiness cannot endure forever. This is why they must be canceled in one stroke! If you do not cancel them yourself, impermanence will come to cancel them, and then birth and death will no longer be under your control. [How much striving in vain]
“Where are the generals and ministers of old and new? A mound of wild grass covers all that's left.”
(The Song of the Good End, from The Dream of the Red Chamber)
[The dream of yellow millet] An allusion from the Tang dynasty Record Within the Pillow:
“In the seventh year of the Kaicheng reign, there was a student of the Lu family, named Ying, styled Cuizhi. At an inn in Handan
(an inn)

, he met the Daoist Old Man Lü. The student sighed deeply over his poverty and hardship, and the old man took a pillow from his bag and gave it to him, saying: ‘Pillow your head on this pillow of mine, and I shall make you honored, distinguished, and content!’ At that moment the innkeeper was just steaming millet
(yellow millet)

, and the student lowered his head onto the pillow and fell into a dream within it. He returned to his home, and within a few months married a daughter of the Cui family of Qinghe. The wife was exceedingly beautiful, and the dowry
(marriage portion)
grew ever richer, and the student was overjoyed. Then, soon
(before long)
, he passed the jinshi examination and rose through offices to be a secretariat drafter
(accumulating merit and rising to be a drafter of the Central Secretariat)
, and was transferred to be a military governor
(promoted to military governor)
, and routed the barbarians, becoming chancellor
(serving as chancellor)
for more than ten years. His five sons all held office
(became officials)
, and his ten-odd grandsons, through their marriages
(in-laws)
, were all connected with the most eminent families of the realm
(illustrious clans)
, and he died at over eighty
(zú: passed away)
. When he awoke, the millet was not yet cooked. Astonished
(amazed)
, he said: ‘Could it have been a dream
(could this be a dream)
?’ The old man laughed and said: ‘The fortunes of a man's life
(circumstances)
are just like this!’ The student stood dazed
(at a loss)
for a long while, then bowed deeply in thanks and left.”

[Yellow millet] Yellow grain. [Circumstances] One's fortunes (usually good ones). [Bow deeply] To kneel, cup one's hands to the ground, and lower the head to the ground. [When the dream of yellow millet wakes, look and see what remains] In the Record Within the Pillow, once one wakes, the renown and riches of the dream are all gone. But in real life, when life ends, the result is: of all things, none can be taken along (nothing at all can be carried away); only karma follows the body. [Of all things, none can be taken along; only karma follows the body] People chase fame and profit, not knowing cause and effect, not understanding offense and blessing, and the consequences are most severe. As it is said:
“Fortune and misfortune have no gate; they are summoned only by oneself. The retribution of good and evil follows like a shadow after the form.”
Therefore one must know causes and discern effects, so as to seek good fortune and avoid calamity. The ancient worthies said:
“When a person does good, though blessing has not yet come, calamity has already drawn far away; when a person does evil, though calamity has not yet come, blessing has already drawn far away.”

“Richer than princes and lords — you call it joy, I call it sorrow. The seeker endures much hardship; the gainer fears ruin. Cha! Plain rice surpasses rare delicacies, patched robes are like embroidery. Heaven and earth are my cottage — what need to build great mansions? Therefore house, land, and garden are canceled in one stroke.”

Richer than princes and lords — you say I am joyful, I say it is sorrow: in seeking it, one endures a thousand hardships; having gained it, one fears ruin. Cha! Coarse tea and plain rice surpass rare delicacies; patched robes and worn jackets are like embroidered brocade. Heaven and earth are my house — what need to build great mansions? Therefore house, land, and garden are canceled in one stroke.

[You call it joy, I call it sorrow] You think that because I am richer than princes and lords I must be greatly delighted, not knowing the bitterness within: in pursuit of wealth I endured a thousand hardships; and if by luck I grew rich, I am ever anxious that officials, thieves, flood, fire, or a prodigal son may ruin my wealth. [Endure] To suffer; to toil.

blocks.text: 6. The Chapter on Talent and Learning

inline.s: “The sea of learning flows forever; the array of letters shines up to the Dipper and the Herd-boy star. One roams amid the hundred arts, and at a gallon of wine, a thousand poems. Cha! Brocade fills your breast — why boast? Before birth and death, it cannot save you in the least; therefore world-surpassing writing is canceled in one stroke.”

The sea of learning flows without rest; the literary arena's radiance shines to the Dipper and the Herd-boy; one roams at will amid the hundred arts, and at a gallon of wine, a thousand poems. Cha! Brocade fills your breast — why boast? Before birth and death, not a thread of it can save you; therefore world-surpassing writing is canceled in one stroke.
[The sea of learning] In the Han dynasty, Yang Xiong's Model Sayings

, “Learning and Conduct,” it says: “The hundred rivers, learning from the sea, reach the sea; the hills, learning from the mountain, do not reach the mountain.” This means: the hundred rivers flow without ceasing, and so reach the sea; the hills stand still and do not move, and so do not reach the mountain. Therefore, in pursuing learning one should be like rivers flowing toward the sea, advancing day by day without cease. [The array of letters] The literary arena.
[The array of letters shines up to the Dipper and the Herd-boy star] A description of the height of a person's talent and learning: in the literary arena his radiance is boundless
, shining up to the Dipper (the Northern Dipper) and the Herd-boy star (the Altair star).

blocks.text: 7. The Chapter on Pleasure and Amusement

inline.s: “Summer outings and spring excursions, pleasures crowd the halls of song and dance; mist and rain blur the flowers and willows, chess and wine delight kin and friends. Cha! Before your eyes you flaunt your charm, but the suffering returns after death. What a pity to waste the light, ashamed and empty when you turn to look back; therefore the feelings of romance are canceled in one stroke.”

Summer outings and spring excursions, pleasures crowd the halls of song and dance; mist and rain blur the flowers and willows, tea, wine, qin, and chess delight kin and friends. Cha! Before their eyes each one flaunts his charm, but the suffering returns to oneself after death. What a pity to waste the light and miss the great matter of birth and death; in shame and regret one turns to look back in vain; therefore the feelings of romance are canceled in one stroke.

[Before one's eyes] At present, now, the present time. [Charm (fengliu)] Having both achievement and literary refinement. [Ashamed (mǒ luó)] Sanskrit, translated as “ashamed.” [Turn to look back in vain] Looking back on past affairs, all is emptiness.

Time passes swiftly and human life is impermanent. Students of the Buddha must be alert at all times, and by no means take it lightly, indulging in play and amusement and squandering the time, only to regret it endlessly. Samantabhadra Bodhisattva's Verse Admonishing the Assembly says:
“This day is already past
(this day is now over)
, and life decreases with it
(the days one lives in this world decrease by one accordingly)
, like a fish in dwindling water
(like a fish in a pond whose water dries up day by day)
— what joy is there in this
(what joy can there be)
? O great assembly! Strive diligently
(you should practice with diligence and vigor)
, as if saving your head from burning
as urgently as if saving your own head, without a moment's delay
. Only be mindful of impermanence
(think at every moment of the coming of death)
, and be not heedless
(by no means let yourself go, craving ease and comfort and wasting this precious time)
[Strive diligently, as if saving your head from burning] You should practice with diligence and vigor,
as urgently as if saving your own head, without a moment's delay. (For example, when something comes hurtling toward your head, you must block it at once, or dodge it,
without a moment's delay
. Likewise, when death strikes, the practice that liberates this body must be
diligent and vigorous,
without a moment's delay
.) “Ran” is used at the end of a word to indicate a state, as in “xianran” (evidently), “huran” (suddenly), “piaopiaoran” (floatingly).
This sentence means: death is swiftly approaching, so in reciting the Buddha's name one should be
diligent and unremitting,
and quickly
impatiently, before unconsciousness and death overtake one,
accomplish “the ten recitations in continuity, until habit becomes nature”
(see
The Conditions for Rebirth

for details). [Impermanence] Not abiding forever (all dharmas of the world arise and cease in flux, not staying for an instant); also refers to death, the ghost that seizes the soul. [Be not heedless] By no means let yourself go, craving ease and comfort and wasting this precious time. The Buddha said:
“Though one toils for a lifetime, in but an instant afterward one is reborn in the Land of Measureless Life, with joy without limit.”
(The Buddha Speaks the Sūtra of the Buddha of Measureless Life)
Truly:
In life one exhausts a thousand schemes of mind; after death, one leaves but a pair of empty hands behind.
Sorrow and joy, parting and meeting, clamor day after day; long life and early death, want and success, busy each and every day.
Cease to contend for strength and vie for victory; a hundred years is naught but a theater of play.
The moment the gongs and drums fall still, one knows not where the final exit may be.

[Cease to contend for strength and vie for victory] A person's life passes like a white colt glimpsed through a crack in the wall — gone in a blink. Its result is that “nothing at all can be taken along; only karma follows the body”: after death the hands are empty, while the retribution for the evil karma created by contending and vying will follow one like a shadow into the next life. Therefore, cease to contend for strength and vie for victory, and use the energy and time spent on contention in practice to end birth and death. [A hundred years is naught but a theater of play] A life of a hundred years is entirely a play. [The moment the gongs and drums fall still] In a moment the gongs and drums fall silent, and the play is finished (one's life has ended).
